title: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure
subtitle: How one network number learned to cover many cables, using a bit mask.
summary: RFC 950 lets an organization split one IP network number into several subnets by treating some of the host bits as a subnet number. A 32-bit address mask tells each host which bits to compare when it decides whether a destination is on its own cable or needs a gateway. The RFC also adds two ICMP messages, Address Mask Request and Reply, so a newly booted host can learn the mask. It is still an Internet Standard (STD 5), and the mask idea lives on in every IPv4 netmask and prefix length.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 950 lets an organization split one IP network number into several subnets by using some host bits as a subnet number. A 32-bit address mask tells a host which bits to compare when deciding whether a destination is on its own cable or needs a gateway. It also adds two ICMP messages so a booting host can learn the mask. It is still an Internet Standard (STD 5), and the mask idea lives on in IPv4 netmasks.

questions: how does a host know if an address is on the local network
what are icmp address mask request and reply
why can't the subnet field be all zeros or all ones
how did subnetting work before cidr

tldr.problem: Organizations with several LANs needed many network numbers or awkward bridging, which bloated Internet routing tables.
tldr.mechanism: Treat part of the host bits as a subnet number, and give every host a 32-bit address mask to compare against when deciding local versus gateway delivery.
tldr.outcome: One network number can cover many cables while the outside world sees a single network. The mask idea became the IPv4 netmask and, with CIDR, the prefix length.

today: Every IPv4 interface still has an address mask, whether written as 255.255.255.0 or as a prefix length such as /24. Operating systems apply the same bitwise-AND test shown in this RFC to decide between on-link delivery and a gateway. Classful network numbers have since given way to CIDR (RFC 4632), and hosts usually learn their mask from DHCP (RFC 2131) rather than the ICMP Address Mask messages, which are now rarely used.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Early IP addresses had two levels: a network number, then a host number. Each network was a "black box" to everyone outside it. That worked until organizations such as universities grew past a single cable. RFC 950 describes a third level in the middle: a subnet, one of several cables or LANs that share a single Internet network number.

The RFC is written mainly for hosts such as workstations. It says plainly that the procedures "used in and between subnet gateways are not fully described". It builds on RFC 917, "Internet Subnets", and takes its motivation from RFC 940.

RFC 950 is part of STD 5, together with RFC 791 (IP), RFC 792 (ICMP), RFC 919, RFC 922 and RFC 1112. It formally updates RFC 792 by adding two ICMP message types.
sections.plainLanguage: Early IP addresses had two levels: a network number and a host number. RFC 950 adds a middle level, the subnet, so several cables or LANs can share one Internet network number. It is written mainly for hosts and does not fully describe the procedures between subnet gateways. It updates RFC 792 by adding two ICMP message types.

sections.title: Why subnets
sections.content:
The RFC gives four reasons why one organization might need more than one cable: different LAN technologies (for example Ethernet and a ring network), electrical limits on cable length and host count, congestion that is relieved by putting chatty groups on separate cables, and point-to-point links between sites too far apart for one LAN.

Having several cables, the organization has three choices. It can get a separate network number for each cable, which causes "an explosion in the size of Internet routing tables". It can use one number and hide the cables behind bridges ("transparent subnets"), which needs ARP-like tricks, does not work on every LAN technology, and makes bridges track every host. Or it can partition the host address space into subnet numbers ("explicit subnets"). RFC 950 picks the third, accepting that it needs "relatively minor" changes to IP implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: An organization may need several cables because of different LAN technologies, cable length limits, congestion, or distant sites. It could get a network number per cable, which bloats Internet routing tables. It could hide the cables behind bridges, which does not work on every LAN technology. Or it could split the host address space into subnet numbers. RFC 950 chooses this third option.

sections.title: Interpreting addresses
sections.content:
The RFC weighs five ways to carry the subnet number: a variable-width field, a fixed-width field, either of those self-encoding in high bits like the address classes, or an address mask. It chooses the mask, because it is "the most flexible scheme, yet costs no more to implement than any other".

An address is read as <network-number><subnet-number><host-number>. The network number is defined by IP, the host number is at least 1 bit wide, and the subnet field has a constant width on a given network. A width of zero means no subnetting. The subnet bits are chosen by the mask so they need not be adjacent, but the RFC recommends they be contiguous and the most significant bits of the local part.

The subnet values of all zeros and all ones should not be assigned to real subnets, so that "this" and "all" keep their special meanings. With a 6-bit subnet field the legal values are 1 to 62; the RFC's example says any value "except 0 and 63".
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC chooses an address mask as the way to carry the subnet number, because it is the most flexible scheme and costs no more to implement. An address is read as network number, subnet number, then host number. The mask defines the subnet bits, which should be contiguous. Subnet values of all zeros and all ones should not be assigned, so "this" and "all" keep their meanings.

sections.title: Changes to host software
sections.content:
Before subnets, an IP module decided between local delivery and a gateway by comparing network numbers of the destination and itself. With subnets a host stores one more 32-bit value, my_ip_mask, with bits set for the network number and the subnet number. It then compares bitwise_and(dg.ip_dest, my_ip_mask) against bitwise_and(my_ip_addr, my_ip_mask). If they match the datagram is sent directly; otherwise it goes to the gateway for that masked destination.

The RFC notes the gateway_to lookup may also need to take the subnet bits into account. A host with several interfaces keeps an address and mask per interface and evaluates the test for each.
sections.plainLanguage: With subnets, a host stores one more 32-bit value, its mask. To decide on delivery, it applies the mask to the destination address and to its own address. If the results match, the destination is on the same subnet and the host sends the datagram directly. Otherwise it sends it to a gateway. A host with several interfaces keeps an address and mask for each.

sections.title: Finding the address mask
sections.content:
A booting host faces the same bootstrapping problem as finding its own address or a gateway: use hardwired information, or ask by broadcast. Diskless workstations cannot rely on a stored file. The RFC prefers getting all boot facts in one request, for example from a boot server as in RFC 951 (BOOTP), and mentions RARP (RFC 903) for the host's own address.

When the mask must be found separately, the host broadcasts an ICMP Address Mask Request. A gateway, or a host acting in place of one, answers with an Address Mask Reply. Because "there is only one possible value" for a subnet, the host need not match replies to its request, and several replies are harmless. If the request's source address is zero, the reply is broadcast too, though the RFC says to avoid this where possible to limit broadcast load.

If no answer comes after a reasonable number of tries, the host should assume the plain network-number mask. No host or gateway should send a reply based on a guessed value. When a gateway comes up it should broadcast a reply, and a host that guessed wrong should switch to the received mask.
sections.plainLanguage: A booting host must learn its mask from hardwired information or by asking. The RFC prefers getting all boot facts in one request, such as from a boot server (RFC 951, BOOTP). Otherwise the host broadcasts an ICMP Address Mask Request, and a gateway answers with an Address Mask Reply. If no answer comes after reasonable tries, the host should assume the plain network-number mask.

sections.title: The ICMP messages
sections.content:
Appendix I defines one message layout for both Address Mask Request and Reply: Type, Code, Checksum, Identifier, Sequence Number and a 32-bit Address Mask. The type is AM1 for requests and AM2 for replies; Appendix IV assigns AM1 = 17 and AM2 = 18. Code is 0 for both. The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the ICMP message starting with the Type, computed with the checksum field zeroed. Identifier and Sequence Number may be zero and may be ignored.

To build a reply the gateway swaps the source and destination addresses, sets the type to AM2, inserts the mask for the subnet on which the request arrived, and recomputes the checksum. The request's mask field is sent as 0.
sections.plainLanguage: One message layout serves both ICMP messages: Type, Code, Checksum, Identifier, Sequence Number and a 32-bit Address Mask. The type is 17 for a request and 18 for a reply, and the code is 0. To reply, the gateway swaps the addresses, sets the type to 18, inserts the mask for the subnet the request arrived on, and recomputes the checksum.

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.content:
Appendix II walks through three networks. In the Class A case, host 36.40.0.123 on network 36 uses an 8-bit subnet field, giving mask 255.255.0.0, and gateway 36.40.0.62 answers. In the Class B case, host 128.99.4.123 uses a 6-bit field, so the mask is 255.255.252.0. In the Class C case on 192.1.127.0, the mask is 255.255.255.88 (binary 01011000 in the last byte), deliberately showing non-contiguous subnet bits.

Each example shows three variants: a host that knows its address sends the request to 255.255.255.255 and gets a unicast reply; a diskless host that does not yet know its address sends from 0.0.0.0 and gets a broadcast reply; and if broadcasting is not allowed it sends directly to a wired-in gateway address.

Non-contiguous masks like 255.255.255.88 are allowed by RFC 950, which only recommends contiguous subnet bits, and CIDR assumes contiguous prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: Appendix II gives examples for Class A, B and C networks. For host 36.40.0.123 the mask is 255.255.0.0, for 128.99.4.123 it is 255.255.252.0, and for network 192.1.127.0 it is 255.255.255.88. Each shows three cases: a host that knows its address, a diskless host that does not yet and receives a broadcast reply, and a host that cannot broadcast and asks a wired-in gateway address.

fields.desc: The Internet network number, as defined by IP.

fields.desc: Host within the subnet. Must be at least 1 bit wide.

data.title: Outgoing datagram decision with a mask (from RFC 950 §2.2)
data.code:
IF bitwise_and(dg.ip_dest, my_ip_mask)
                          = bitwise_and(my_ip_addr, my_ip_mask)
    THEN
        send_dg_locally(dg, dg.ip_dest)
    ELSE
        send_dg_locally(dg,
               gateway_to(bitwise_and(dg.ip_dest, my_ip_mask)))
